A.basis: Sustained treatment of biological and computational neuron and synapse models and their realism-efficiency trade-offs.

B.basis: Explains binary spike representation and names rate, temporal, and population codes, with little decoding analysis.

C.basis: Compares plasticity, evolutionary search, spike-time gradients, surrogate gradients, backpropagation through time, and online learning.

D.basis: Identifies rate-based ANN-to-SNN conversion and its efficiency limitation without developing conversion methods.

E.basis: No comparative treatment of SNN software frameworks or their model and operator support was identified.

F.basis: Explains partitioning, placement, crossbar realization, limited-precision mapping, and named mapping frameworks.

G.basis: No concrete neuromorphic interchange representation or portable semantic format is analyzed.

H.basis: Sustained coverage of circuits, devices, and analog, digital, mixed-signal, and many-core SNN architectures.

I.basis: Identifies precision mismatch, state-memory pressure, synchronization overhead, noise, variability, and interoperability without a complete semantic taxonomy.

J.basis: Identifies missing standardized benchmarks and distinguishes algorithmic complexity from hardware efficiency, but supplies no evidence classes.

K.basis: Surveys workload families and reports a quantified event-vision mapping result, while most application coverage remains descriptive.

L.basis: Discusses mapping and deployment stages but does not trace one network through a named software stack to measured physical-chip execution.

surveys.strongest_contribution: Hardware-aware mapping tutorial spanning partitioning, placement, crossbars, precision, memory, and synchronization.
surveys.deployment_depth: Explains deployment constraints and mapping stages but provides no complete named framework-to-silicon route.
omissions: No software-framework comparison, interchange format, claim-level evidence taxonomy, or complete network-to-chip route.

A.basis: Explains IF, LIF, bio-plausible neuron and synapse models, and implementation costs.

B.basis: Compares rate, TTFS, and inter-spike-interval coding and connects coding to timing error and hardware activity.
B.locator: Section 2.2, pp. 4-5; Sections 4.3 and 7.1, pp. 14-15 and 25

C.basis: Compares STDP, reward modulation, supervised learning, spike-domain backpropagation, and training location.

D.basis: Reviews conversion frameworks, topology modification, rate-coding cost, temporal conversion, and an accuracy-loss example.

E.basis: No software-framework ecosystem or simulator comparison was identified.

F.basis: Compares depth-wise and spatial mapping, load balance, communication distance, and graph-based optimization without toolchain coverage.

G.basis: No interchange representation or portable graph format is analyzed.

H.basis: Covers analog and digital neurocores, crossbars, large-scale systems, and embedded accelerators.

I.basis: Explains mapping imbalance, timing error, input-conversion bias, topology dependence, precision loss, and device non-idealities.

J.basis: Explicitly distinguishes simulated, FPGA, and fabricated technologies and flags incomparable model types and missing data.

K.basis: Provides accuracy, energy, area, and coding data for low-power image-classification accelerators, mainly on MNIST.

L.basis: Table 2 connects training and input conversion to topology, implementation, and energy, without a reproducible software-to-chip workflow.

surveys.strongest_contribution: Joint algorithm-hardware analysis with unusually explicit accelerator evidence labels and benchmark caveats.
surveys.deployment_depth: Compact hardware route summaries for several accelerators, without modern framework or compiler paths.
omissions: No software-framework survey, interchange format, modern compiler comparison, or general evidence taxonomy.

A.basis: Derives conductance-based and spike-based models and connects their dynamics to implementation.

B.basis: Compares rate, TTFS, phase, and task-specific codes with latency, spike-count, quantization, and hardware trade-offs.

C.basis: Covers STDP, supervised Hebbian learning, spike-domain backpropagation, local credit assignment, and online-learning limits.
C.locator: Section II-E, pp. 13-14; Section V-A, pp. 25-26

D.basis: Notes Nengo-based DNN-to-SNN conversion for Loihi and Tianjic indirect training without reviewing conversion algorithms.
D.locator: Section IV-B.3, p. 21; Section IV-E.5, p. 24

E.basis: Distinguishes mapping, programming, and simulation tools and compares platform-specific APIs and frameworks.
E.locator: Section III-E, p. 17; Sections IV-A to IV-E, pp. 20-24

F.basis: Explains mapping objectives, Eedn, Loihi compiler stages, PACMAN, and Tianjic's automatic compiler.
F.locator: Section III-E, p. 17; Sections IV-A.3, IV-B.3, IV-D.3, and IV-E.5, pp. 20-24

G.basis: No portable interchange representation or NIR-like semantic format is analyzed.

H.basis: Detailed TrueNorth, Loihi, BrainScaleS, SpiNNaker, and Tianjic case studies and comparative capability tables.

I.basis: Identifies model-support mismatches, time-multiplexing delay, fixed-point limits, routing constraints, and software abstractions.
I.locator: Sections II-C, III, and IV, pp. 10-24

J.basis: Platform tables do not classify results by physical measurement, simulation, or analytical estimate.

K.basis: Reports measured TrueNorth throughput and power and describes Loihi and Tianjic applications, without systematic application tables.
K.locator: Sections IV-A.3, IV-B.3, and IV-E.6, pp. 20-24

L.basis: TrueNorth Eedn and Tianjic discussions connect training or mapping support to named hardware and applications without complete reproducibility details.

surveys.strongest_contribution: Algorithm-hardware co-design survey with substantive, platform-specific software and compiler coverage.
surveys.deployment_depth: Connects model semantics, software abstractions, compilers, and named platform applications, but not as one reproducible route.
omissions: No interchange format, claim-level evidence taxonomy, cross-platform route comparison, or detailed conversion taxonomy.

A.basis: Covers HH, IF, LIF, memristive Izhikevich, and major SNN topologies with hardware context.

B.basis: Identifies spikes as spatiotemporal codes and temporal coding as a circuit trade-off without a coding taxonomy.

C.basis: Names STDP, temporal backpropagation, surrogate-gradient engines, and on-chip learning support without comparing training methods.

D.basis: No substantive ANN-to-SNN conversion method or conversion-error analysis was identified.

E.basis: Names NEST and Brian 2 while diagnosing the lack of integrated deployment solutions, without comparing framework capabilities.

F.basis: Mentions programmable mapping and the need for integrated deployment toolchains without explaining a compiler or mapper.

G.basis: No interchange format or portable semantic representation is treated.

H.basis: Sustained comparison of analog-digital hybrid, digital-only, second-generation, and memristor platforms.

I.basis: Compares flexibility, plasticity, timing, scalability, architecture diversity, and integration limits without cross-stack semantic analysis.

J.basis: Uses a five-dimensional comparison and marks some no-data and inferred entries, but does not classify evidence consistently across claims.

K.basis: Broad workload coverage with selected reported power and efficiency results across AI, robotics, neuroscience, and control.

L.basis: Describes a physically mapped memristor reinforcement-learning network and named chip deployments, but omits complete training and measurement chains.

surveys.strongest_contribution: Five-dimensional chip taxonomy and broad workload-oriented application synthesis.
surveys.deployment_depth: Names several physical deployments and one mapped memristor workload, without complete compiler and measurement provenance.
omissions: No conversion treatment, framework or compiler comparison, interchange format, or consistently applied evidence classification.
